headings.title: Physiological Changes and Nutritional Demands in Adolescence
headings.content: Adolescence marks a period of rapid physical growth second only to infancy. During this developmental window, adolescents experience a major growth spurt involving skeletal expansion, muscle mass accumulation, and development of reproductive organs. These dramatic bodily changes cause a sharp rise in energy and nutrient requirements. For girls, the onset of menarche introduces regular blood loss, fundamentally altering physiological needs. Nurses caring for this demographic must recognize that standard childhood dietary guidelines no longer suffice to support their active biological development.

headings.title: Essential Micronutrients: Iron, Calcium, and Folic Acid
headings.content:
- **Iron**: Essential for hemoglobin formation to prevent iron-deficiency anemia, particularly vital given the onset of menstrual losses.
- **Calcium**: Crucial for peak bone mass accumulation, helping to prevent osteoporosis later in life.
- **Folic Acid**: Necessary for DNA synthesis and cell division, holding preventative importance for future neural tube defects if pregnancy occurs.

headings.title: Macronutrient Balance and Energy Needs
headings.content: Adolescent girls require an appropriate balance of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats to fuel daily activities and support organ development. Carbohydrates should provide the bulk of daily calories, focusing on complex, fiber-rich sources like unpolished local grains and tubers rather than refined sugars. Proteins support tissue synthesis and muscle growth, while healthy fats are necessary for hormone production and fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Caloric needs vary depending on physical activity levels, but restricting energy intake to achieve thinness harms normal development and cognitive function.

headings.title: Prevalent Nutritional Deficiencies in Nigerian Settings
headings.content: Nutritional surveys across Nigeria highlight specific deficiencies affecting adolescent girls disproportionately. Iron-deficiency anemia remains widespread due to cereal-based diets low in bioavailable heme iron combined with blood loss from menstruation and parasitic infections like hookworm. Protein-energy malnutrition often manifests as chronic undernutrition or stunting in vulnerable communities. Additionally, micronutrient deficiencies such as vitamin A and zinc shortfalls impair immune function and delay growth. Socioeconomic constraints and household food distribution practices frequently exacerbate these deficiencies.

headings.title: Socio-Cultural Factors Affecting Dietary Choices
headings.content: Dietary habits during adolescence are heavily shaped by peer pressure, media influences, and traditional cultural norms. Body image ideals promoted by modern media often drive adolescent girls to adopt restrictive dieting behaviors, skipping meals in pursuit of thinness. Conversely, local food taboos in certain Nigerian communities may restrict girls from consuming nutrient-dense items like eggs, meats, or certain fish. Understanding these cultural dynamics allows nurses to deliver culturally sensitive counseling rather than imposing unrealistic dietary changes.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment in Clinical Practice
headings.content: Conducting a comprehensive nutritional assessment for an adolescent requires combining anthropometric measurements, biochemical tests, clinical signs, and dietary history. Body mass index-for-age charts help identify underweight, overweight, or stunting. Nurses look for physical signs of malnutrition such as pallor, brittle hair, or swollen gums. Dietary recall methods uncover eating patterns, meal skipping, and food avoidance. Accurate assessment establishes a baseline and guides targeted interventions.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Dietary Counselling
headings.content: Nursing management focuses on empowering adolescent girls and their families through practical nutrition education. Counselling sessions should promote affordable, locally available food sources like beans, groundnuts, green leafy vegetables, and iron-fortified staples. Nurses should encourage positive body image discussions and dispel myths surrounding weight control. Collaborating with school health programs extends the reach of nutritional interventions to a broader community of young girls.
